body:
Agriculture as the Economic Foundation

Agriculture was central to the economy of the Mauryan period. The production of grain and other crops supported rural households, provided food for towns and supplied an important part of state revenue.

Productive agriculture also supported occupations that were not directly concerned with farming. Soldiers, administrators, merchants and specialised artisans depended on food produced by cultivators.

The relationship between agriculture and the state was therefore close. The ruler wanted reliable agricultural output because it supported the population and made revenue collection possible.

Iron Tools and Agricultural Expansion

The increasing use of iron tools was an important development in early Indian agriculture. Iron axes could help clear suitable land, while iron-tipped ploughshares were useful for cultivating fertile soils.

Plough agriculture expanded in parts of the fertile river valleys, including the Ganga valley, from approximately the 6th century BCE. This development began before the establishment of the Mauryan Empire and continued during the early historic period.

Iron tools were not used uniformly across the subcontinent. In some hilly regions, cultivators continued to use hoes because they were better suited to the terrain. Local rainfall, soils and available resources influenced farming methods.

Paddy Transplantation

Transplantation involves growing young paddy plants and then moving them to prepared, waterlogged fields. Under suitable conditions, this method can improve plant survival and crop yields.

It also requires substantial labour. Increased agricultural output therefore did not mean that cultivation became easy for every worker.

The spread of transplantation in suitable parts of the Ganga valley contributed to increased agricultural production. However, it depended on adequate water and was not appropriate for every region or crop.

The Importance of Irrigation

Rainfall was a major source of water for crops, but irrigation helped cultivators manage water availability more effectively.

Early irrigation arrangements included:

  • Wells: Sources of water for fields and settlements.
  • Tanks: Structures that stored water for later use.
  • Canals: Channels that carried water from a source to cultivated land.
  • Artificial reservoirs: Larger stores of water that could supply irrigation systems.

Such works could support cultivation, reduce dependence on uncertain rainfall and improve agricultural output where local conditions allowed.

Irrigation facilities were not necessarily constructed only by kings. Communities, private individuals and powerful local authorities also organised irrigation works. Royal construction was one important form of support, not the only form.

State-Managed Agriculture

The Arthashastra describes land and agricultural activities directly managed by the state. The term sita is associated with this form of cultivation, while the sitadhyaksha was the superintendent responsible for state agriculture.

State-managed lands could involve the supervision of cultivation, labour, crops and agricultural supplies. They must be distinguished from fields cultivated by independent landholders from whom the ruler collected a share of produce.

It would be incorrect to conclude from the Arthashastra that the Mauryan state owned and directly cultivated every field in the empire.

The Sudarshana Lake: A Major Gujarat Connection

The Sudarshana Lake was an artificial reservoir near Girnar in present-day Junagadh, Gujarat. It is an important example of irrigation and the connection between provincial administration and public works.

The history of the reservoir is known particularly from a later inscription of Rudradaman I, dated to approximately 150 CE. This inscription records events associated with the earlier Mauryan period.

Construction Under Chandragupta Maurya

According to the Junagadh inscription, the reservoir was constructed by Pushyagupta, an administrator serving under Chandragupta Maurya.

The record identifies Pushyagupta as a Vaishya and connects him with the government of the region. His involvement shows that important public works could be undertaken through provincial administration.

Water Channels Under Ashoka

The inscription also refers to Tushaspha, a Yavana official associated with Ashoka's administration, who arranged water channels connected with the reservoir.

Thus, the record distinguishes the original construction of the reservoir under Chandragupta from the development of channels under Ashoka.

Later Repair Under Rudradaman

Much later, during the rule of Rudradaman I, heavy rainfall damaged the reservoir's embankment. His inscription records the repair of the structure.

This later repair is important because it shows that irrigation facilities established in one political period could remain economically important under subsequent rulers.

Distinguish the inscriptions at Girnar

Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts at Girnar belong to the Mauryan period and were composed mainly in Prakrit using Brahmi. Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription, composed in Sanskrit around 150 CE, is later evidence describing the earlier history and repair of Sudarshana Lake. They are not the same inscription.

Why the Lake Matters for Understanding the Economy

Water storage and distribution could support farming beyond the immediate dependence on rainfall. More reliable agricultural production could benefit cultivators, sustain settlements and increase the resources available to the state.

The Sudarshana Lake also demonstrates an important administrative principle: the economic development of a province could involve local governors and officials acting under the authority of the emperor.

Prelims focus

  • Iron-tipped ploughshares and paddy transplantation supported agricultural expansion in suitable regions.
  • Wells, tanks, canals and reservoirs were important irrigation arrangements.
  • Sitadhyaksha was associated with the supervision of state agriculture in the Arthashastra.
  • Sudarshana Lake was located near Girnar in present-day Junagadh, Gujarat.
  • Pushyagupta is associated with its construction under Chandragupta; Tushaspha with water channels under Ashoka.
  • Trap: The inscription recording these Mauryan works was issued by the later ruler Rudradaman around 150 CE.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, 'A Changing Countryside', printed pp. 38–40, including 'The Sudarshana Lake in Gujarat'; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 9, 'Vital Villages, Thriving Towns', printed pp. 87–89; IGNOU, 'Economy of the Mauryan Period', Unit 19, sections on agriculture and state production; Rudradaman I, Junagadh rock inscription, c. 150 CE, F. Kielhorn, Epigraphia Indica, Volume 8, no. 6, pp. 42–49, digital text consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: Agriculture, Irrigation and the Sudarshana Lake of Gujarat

body:
Growth of Towns and Commercial Activity

The rise of the Mauryan Empire was closely connected with broader economic changes that had begun before Mauryan rule. From approximately the 6th century BCE, towns expanded in several parts of the subcontinent, especially along important routes of communication.

Some towns were political capitals, while others became important for trade, crafts or access to resources. A single town could perform several functions.

Pataliputra was both a political centre and an important settlement on the Ganga. Taxila connected the northwest with routes towards Central Asia. Ujjayini occupied an important position on routes linking northern India with western and southern regions.

Why Towns and Villages Depended on Each Other

Most towns could not produce all the food they required. Agricultural villages supplied grain, other food products and some raw materials. Urban artisans converted raw materials into finished goods, while merchants transported and exchanged products.

For example, farmers produced cotton, textile workers processed fibres and wove cloth, and traders carried finished textiles to markets. This illustrates the relationship between agriculture, crafts and trade.

Such exchanges also supported the state. Markets, trade routes and commercial transactions provided opportunities to collect tolls and other duties.

Important Urban Crafts

The early historic economy included a variety of specialised occupations:

  • Blacksmiths: Produced iron tools and other metal objects.
  • Carpenters: Worked with timber for buildings, vehicles and other products.
  • Potters: Produced vessels used in households and trade.
  • Weavers and textile workers: Produced cloth from fibres such as cotton.
  • Goldsmiths and other metalworkers: Produced ornaments and specialised goods.
  • Merchants: Organised the movement and sale of raw materials and finished products.

These occupations demonstrate that the economy consisted of much more than farming. Urban demand helped sustain specialised production, while rural output helped maintain towns.

Northern Black Polished Ware

Northern Black Polished Ware, commonly abbreviated as NBPW, is a distinctive fine pottery associated with the early historic period.

It is known for its carefully made, often glossy surface. The ware appears in the period of early urban growth and continued during Mauryan times.

NBPW is useful as evidence of specialised pottery production and the circulation of fine goods. However, it did not originate only after the Mauryan Empire was founded.

Shrenis: Associations of Artisans and Merchants

Artisans and merchants increasingly formed associations called shrenis, commonly described as guilds.

Guilds could help members obtain raw materials, organise production, train workers and market finished goods. Merchant associations could help organise commercial activities.

In the broader early historic period, some guilds also performed financial functions, including receiving deposits and supporting religious institutions. The evidence for these activities spans several centuries, so every later function should not automatically be assigned to Mauryan guilds.

Trade Routes and the State

Trade depended on routes that connected producers and consumers. The Ganga and other rivers provided routes for moving goods. Roads connected inland settlements, political centres and markets.

Merchants transported goods such as grain, salt, cloth, metals, timber and other products. These goods could be exchanged within a region or carried over longer distances.

Controlling important routes helped the state maintain political authority. It also created opportunities to protect movement, supervise trade and collect duties.

Punch-Marked Coins and Exchange

Punch-marked coins were among the earliest coins used in the Indian subcontinent. They appeared from approximately the 6th century BCE and circulated during Mauryan times.

They were generally made of metals such as silver or copper and carried symbols impressed with punches. They did not normally display the names and portraits of rulers.

Coins facilitated some exchanges, but the economy did not depend exclusively on money. Payments and transactions could also involve produce and other goods.

Punch-marked coinage must be distinguished from later Indo-Greek coins, which are especially important for the appearance of rulers' names and images. The introduction of punch-marked coins therefore predates the Mauryan Empire.

Economic Superintendents in the Arthashastra

The Arthashastra describes officials responsible for supervising important economic activities.

OfficialArea of supervision
PanyadhyakshaCommerce and the handling or sale of goods.
ShulkadhyakshaTolls and customs duties.
PautavadhyakshaWeights and measures.
AkaradhyakshaMines and mining-related activities.
SitadhyakshaState-managed agricultural production.

These proposed offices show the attention given to market supervision, reliable measurement and control of valuable resources.

They do not mean that every craft workshop, shop or agricultural field was operated directly by the state. Private producers, merchants and associations remained important parts of the economy.

Prelims focus

  • Pataliputra was important on the Ganga; Taxila and Ujjayini were associated with major routes.
  • NBPW refers to fine Northern Black Polished Ware pottery.
  • Shrenis were associations of artisans or merchants.
  • Punch-marked coins were in use before the Mauryan Empire and continued during it.
  • Shulkadhyaksha was associated with tolls; Pautavadhyaksha with weights and measures.
  • Trap: Early historic trade with the Roman world in later centuries should not automatically be treated as evidence of Mauryan-period trade.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 9, 'Vital Villages, Thriving Towns', printed pp. 87–95; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, 'Towns and Trade', printed pp. 42–45; IGNOU, 'Economy of the Mauryan Period', Unit 19, sections on crafts, trade and urban activity; Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book II, chapters on commerce, customs, weights and measures and mines, R. Shamasastry translation, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: Towns, Crafts, Trade Routes and Economic Regulation
